Prescott's title (and thus the title of the book) also refers to Peabody. While Groton did not use the term "rector" for its headmaster (the term was instead used by [[St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)|St. Paul's School]]), the school community informally referred to Endicott Peabody as "''the'' Rector".<ref>''Views from the Circle'', p. 64.</ref>

==== Other characters ====
The character of Brian Aspinwall is modeled on Auchincloss' old mentor, Malcolm Strachan.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=61}} Auchincloss admitted that Aspinwall was "much weaker and less attractive ... than Malcolm had ever been", but rejected claims that the character was a veiled attack on Strachan.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=61}} He said that he wanted to make Aspinwall as different from Prescott as possible for dramatic effect.{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=60}}

Auchincloss based Prescott's friend Horace Havistock on [[University of Cambridge]] legal historian [[G. T. Lapsley]].<ref name=":12" /> Like Havistock, Lapsley was a gay man<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Annan |first=Noel |author-link=Noel Annan, Baron Annan |date=1990 |title=The Cult of Homosexuality in England 1850—1950 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23539516 |journal=[[Biography (journal)|Biography]] |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=194 |issn=0162-4962 |via=JSTOR}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Bell |first=Millicent |date=July 19, 1984 |title=Notes of a Friend and Brother |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1984/07/19/notes-of-a-friend-and-brother/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250424065030/https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1984/07/19/notes-of-a-friend-and-brother/ |archive-date=April 24, 2025 |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=31 |issue=12 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref> who left America for Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gaillard Thomas Lapsley |url=http://trinitycollegechapel.com/about/memorials/brasses/lapsley/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |website=Trinity College, Cambridge |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215953/http://trinitycollegechapel.com/about/memorials/brasses/lapsley/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Themes ==
Auchincloss spent most of his career detailing the decline of [[White Anglo-Saxon Protestants]]' (WASPs) leading role in American society.{{efn|Auchincloss personally disliked the term "WASP" and preferred the term "Protestant."<ref name=":17" />}} Shortly before his death, he explained that while most of his WASP friends were ''richer'' in the 21st century than they had been growing up, "everyone has moved up", and the old-money elite had "lost their monopoly."<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |title=Louis Auchincloss: The Rector of Justin |url=https://americanlegends.com/Interviews/rector_of_justin.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250713114004/https://americanlegends.com/Interviews/rector_of_justin.html |archive-date=2025-07-13 |access-date=2025-09-27 |website=American Legends}}</ref><ref name=":18">{{Cite news |last=Garner |first=Dwight |author-link=Dwight Garner |date=2010-12-15 |title=A Man Who Knew the People Who Mattered, and Wrote About Them |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/15/books/15book.html |access-date=2025-09-27 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en |archive-date=January 20, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120015523/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/15/books/15book.html}}</ref> He added that "to have witnessed the disintegration of an economic ruling class in the 1930s from a front row seat ... was all a novelist could ask [for]."{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=167}} In an early chapter of ''The Rector of Justin'', Horace Havistock concedes that "the world of the private school" is necessarily tied up with "the world of personal honor and a Protestant God", and that "when a civilization crumbles, it crumbles all together."{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=63}}

=== The collapse of aristocratic values ===
[[File:Former head of New York Stock Exchange before Senate Committee. Washington D.C. Richard Whitney; former President of the New York Stock Exchange, was the first witness as the Senate LCCN2016871192 (cropped).jpg|left|thumb|259x259px|The public disgrace of [[Richard Whitney (financier)|Richard Whitney]] (pictured), the aristocratic president of the [[New York Stock Exchange]], shocked upper-class society.<ref name=":13" />|alt=Photo of Richard Whitney, a disgraced upper-class financier]]
''The Rector of Justin'' explores the erosion of the WASPs' self-belief that values instilled at schools like Groton entitled them to leadership roles in the corporate world and public service, and reflects Auchincloss' growing disillusionment with WASP society in the 1930s and 1940s. Auchincloss said that when he was growing up, the [[Eastern Establishment]] thought it "could be trusted to regulate itself".<ref name=":13" /> As an example of these values, the novel notes how after David Griscam's father went bankrupt and fled the country, his mother felt a "sacred duty" to pay off her absentee husband's debts, forcing the family to abandon its upper-class lifestyle.{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=130}} As a young man, Auchincloss resented the Groton-educated [[Franklin Delano Roosevelt]]'s use of government to enforce morality in the corporate sphere, reasoning that it was a repudiation of Establishment values.<ref name=":13" /> However, he eventually lost faith in the idea that WASPs were more moral than the general population. Another Groton alumnus, financier [[Richard Whitney (financier)|Richard Whitney]], shocked high society with his 1938 [[embezzlement]] conviction;<ref name=":13" /> Auchincloss explored Whitney's misdeeds in his next novel, ''The Embezzler'' (1966).{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=125}} 

{{Quote box
| quote = Pa and Mother, of course, were supreme at Justin, but from the beginning we knew that Justin was not the real world. ... [A]lthough [the real world] treated Pa and Mother with respect, it was the kind of respect that people might pay to the sovereigns of a small Pacific Island kingdom, more exotic than powerful, not quite to be taken seriously, perhaps even a bit ridiculous.
| author = Cordelia Prescott Turnbull
| source = in ''The Rector of Justin'' (chapter 12){{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=179}}
| align = right
| width = 300px
}}

Over the course of the novel, an increasingly immoral WASP establishment begins hiding behind moral individuals like Francis Prescott to obscure its own failures. Auchincloss wrote that the basic idea of the novel was "to study a saint and to leave it up to the reader whether saints are good or bad."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=9}} By the end of the novel, Justinians have raised up an idealized version of Prescott to pretend that Christian values are still relevant to modern society, turning Prescott into "a symbol rather than a source of morality."{{sfn|Piket|1989|p=190}} Prescott's daughter Cordelia points out that the true elites have carefully sidelined her father, who was "not quite to be taken seriously".{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=179}}

Removing Prescott from the picture clarifies that while the American elite's "inviolable rules of conduct ... were once the glue that held together a stern, but deeply felt system of ethical values," by the 1940s they were "little more than useful justifications for preserving a selfish status quo."<ref name="Kakutani">{{Cite news |last=Kakutani |first=Michiko |author-link=Michiko Kakutani |date=1984-07-26 |title=Books of the Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/07/26/books/books-of-the-times-088814.html |access-date=2025-10-06 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> Auchincloss praised the writings of [[Oliver La Farge]], another unhappy Groton alumnus, which taught him that "Groton without Peabody" is "''just'' this 'dream', this stuffy little group of snooty, cruel boys".<ref name=":13" />{{Sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=51-53}} 

Auchincloss' views evolved after the novel was published. After watching his high school classmates [[William Bundy|William]] and [[McGeorge Bundy]] lead America into the [[Vietnam War]], he concluded that the novel's take on Groton ("that its graduates were ... too shallow to aspire to the school's ideals") was fundamentally incorrect. He decided that "the ideals themselves were rotten",<ref name=":13" /> explaining that Groton taught the Bundys to never concede defeat, even when the war could not be won.{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=71}} In ''The House of the Prophet'' (1980), the novel's stand-in for [[Walter Lippmann]] comments that the danger of Groton was in its culture of "pugnacity".<ref name=":13" />

=== Elite decadence ===
[[File:Theodore Roosevelt by the Pach Bros.jpg|alt=Photo of Theodore Roosevelt, a supporter of Endicott Peabody|thumb|262x262px|[[Endicott Peabody (educator)|Endicott Peabody]]'s friend [[Theodore Roosevelt]] supported Peabody's goal to toughen up the children of American elites,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Endicott Peabody |url=https://www.theodorerooseveltcenter.org/Learn-About-TR/TR-Encyclopedia/Culture-and-Society/Endicott-Peabody |access-date=April 23, 2025 |website=Theodore Roosevelt Center |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220028/https://www.theodorerooseveltcenter.org/Learn-About-TR/TR-Encyclopedia/Culture-and-Society/Endicott-Peabody |url-status=live }}</ref> urging Peabody's students to avoid "the life of mere vapid ease."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roosevelt |first=Theodore |date=May 24, 1904 |title=Address at the Prize Day Exercises, Groton School |url=https://americanliterature.com/history/theodore-roosevelt/speech/address-at-the-prize-day-exercises-groton-school |access-date=April 23, 2025 |website=americanliterature.com |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215943/https://americanliterature.com/history/theodore-roosevelt/speech/address-at-the-prize-day-exercises-groton-school |url-status=live }}</ref> However, some students questioned whether Peabody had been successful.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />]]
The novel reflects Auchincloss' disillusionment with American boarding schools' inability to live up to their founders' vision. In a 1968 essay,{{efn|Later reprinted as an afterword to the 2001 Modern Library edition of the novel.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Auchincloss |first=Louis |title=The Rector of Justin |publisher=[[Random House]] |year=2001 |edition=Modern Library |location=New York |chapter=Afterword: Origin of a Hero |pages=355–363}}</ref>}} Auchincloss explained that "the central problem in all New England Protestant church schools of [Peabody's] day was the conflict between the piety and idealism of their inspirers and the crass materialism of the families" that supported them.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=4}} As [[Gore Vidal]] ([[Phillips Exeter Academy|Exeter]] '43) put it, Auchincloss' books frequently trace "the collapse of the Puritan ethical system and its replacement by—as far as those of us now living can tell—nothing."<ref name=":22">{{Cite news |last=Vidal |first=Gore |author-link=Gore Vidal |date=July 18, 1974 |title=Real Class |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1974/07/18/real-class/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250227225750/https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1974/07/18/real-class/ |archive-date=February 27, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=21 |issue=12 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref>

Like Prescott, the real-life Endicott Peabody sought to toughen up spoiled aristocrats through harsh discipline and simple living.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Hicks |first=David V. |date=Autumn 1996 |title=The Strange Fate of the American Boarding School |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41212553 |journal=[[The American Scholar (magazine)|The American Scholar]] |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=525, 528 |jstor=41212553}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bundgaard |first=Axel |title=Muscle and Manliness: The Rise of Sport in American Boarding Schools |publisher=[[Syracuse University Press]] |year=2005 |pages=111–120}}</ref> Auchincloss suggested that this mission was doomed to fail, recalling Peabody "as a [[David]] engaged in the seemingly hopeless struggle of preserving some degree of spirituality from the [[Goliath]] of materialism that re-invaded the school with each new form of prosperous youngsters."<ref name=":14" /> In the novel, Prescott contemptuously remarks that Peabody's Groton is "well equipped to train young men for the steam room of the Racquet Club".<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Peterson |first=Virgilia |date=July 12, 1964 |title=A Crucible Covered with Ivy |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/07/12/archives/a-crucible-covered-with-ivy-the-rector-of-justin-by-louis.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927102305/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/07/12/archives/a-crucible-covered-with-ivy-the-rector-of-justin-by-louis.html |archive-date=September 27, 2022 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Only at the end of his life does Prescott realize that his school is no different.<ref name=":1" />{{efn|[[Nelson W. Aldrich Jr.|Nelson Aldrich]] ([[St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)|St. Paul's]] '53) quipped that while Groton boys dismissed St. Paul's boys as decadent and unworldly, "Groton boys were described in the same terms by Exeter boys, and Exeter boys in (almost) the same terms by high-school boys, and so on ... [until the point where] all boarding-school boys are described, without distinction, as a bunch of fairies."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Aldrich |first=Nelson W. |author-link=Nelson W. Aldrich Jr. |url= |title=Old Money: The Mythology of America's Upper Class |date= |publisher=[[Vintage Books]] |year=1989 |isbn=978-0-679-72224-3 |location=New York |pages=125}}</ref>}}

Auchincloss' upbringing was a case in point. Auchincloss' own father sent him to boarding school out of concern that a child who grew up "in a woman's world of cushions and caresses ... would turn into a sissy".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=36}} But Auchincloss' brother—who was also sent to Groton—left a career in the [[United States Foreign Service|Foreign Service]] for "a life of pleasure and leisure",<ref name=":19">{{Cite news |last=Kaiser |first=Walter |date=March 24, 2011 |title=Inside the Fortress |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2011/03/24/inside-fortress/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=58 |issue=5 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref> and Auchincloss said that "I could have almost lived on what [he] expended on shirts and cufflinks."{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=96}} A lapsed [[Presbyterianism|Presbyterian]], he later wrote that most of his Groton classmates stopped going to church as adults, but hedged that while "the [[Ivy League]] of my day" may have been "godless ... it certainly did not lack ideals".{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=76-78}}

The ending of the novel emphasizes that the American aristocracy must reform to survive. Despite his early ambivalence for the reformist Franklin Roosevelt, Auchincloss later admitted that Roosevelt "was not a traitor to his class" but "its last great representative".<ref name=":13" /> [[Christopher Dahl (administrator)|Christopher Dahl]] writes that the novel's ending suggests "there remains some good in a flawed institution like Justin Martyr, and it is better to support [] mild reforms ... than to abandon the battle altogether."{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=28}}

=== Internal contradictions and self-delusion ===
Despite Prescott's best intentions, he "does not see, and [Aspinwall] only dimly glimpses," that there is a "fundamental irony implicit in attempting to foster 'democratic' ideals in [an upper-class] institution" like Justin Martyr.{{sfn|Parsell|1988|p=49-50}} Auchincloss commented that he "wanted [Prescott] to express the agony of failing ridiculously when he wanted at the very least to fail magnificently".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=5}} He said that Endicott Peabody must have reached a Prescott-like epiphany about his school's failure, explaining that while Peabody must have known that "half the Groton family paid only lip service to his ideals ... and that he had failed to persuade his boys to receive Christ", nobody in the Groton community wanted to admit this to him.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=59-60}} Auchincloss implied that he had gotten this impression from Peabody's confidant Malcolm Strachan.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=59-60}} However, he also wrote that "if Dr. Peabody had his moments of despair, they didn't show."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=5}}

The novel's main characters personify the internal contradictions of WASP society. One of the novel's recurring themes is that "there is something about exclusive boarding schools that magnifies the most juvenile tendencies of adults."{{sfn|Pitofsky|2014|p=58}} Prescott is "a man of intellect and idealism who could be noble, generous and kind but also, by turns, cruel, callous and arbitrary",<ref name=":0" /> and "one of the central strengths of the novel" is that it supports "widely divergent conclusions" about Prescott, with Auchincloss "go[ing] out of his way to present the negative as well as positive aspects of Prescott's character".{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=21}} Christopher Dahl notes that the novel repeatedly provides examples of Prescott's "goodness and spiritual strength, only to follow each of them immediately with an instance of his pettiness or meanness".{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=21}}

[[Robert M. Adams (literary scholar)|Robert M. Adams]] suggested that the book did not make its point clear enough, expressing concern that no individual narrator clearly explained that "a private New England Episcopal prep school [is not a] very distinct alternative to a world of money and snobbery". As an example, he wrote that Aspinwall also displays some of the flaws of the racist and classist trustees who seek to claim Prescott as their own, and that the novel was ultimately "an analysis of a petrified old windbag, unwittingly revealed as such by his most devoted admirer".<ref name=":11">{{Cite news |last=Adams |first=Robert M. |author-link=Robert M. Adams (literary scholar) |date=July 9, 1964 |title=Saturday Night and Sunday Morning |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1964/07/09/saturday-night-and-sunday-morning/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220008/https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1964/07/09/saturday-night-and-sunday-morning/ |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=2 |issue=11 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref> Auchincloss agreed that Aspinwall was a flawed character, commenting that while Aspinwall ends the book resolving to write a biography of Prescott, "personally, I doubt if Brian would have been able to finish it."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=9}}{{sfn|Pitofsky|2014|p=61}}

== Contemporary reception ==

=== Commercial response ===
''The Rector of Justin'' was a major commercial success. It topped the [[List of The New York Times number-one books of 1964|''New York Times'' best-seller list]] for one week,<ref name=":32">{{Cite book |last=Bear |first=John |url= |title=The #1 New York Times Bestseller |date= |publisher=[[Ten Speed Press]] |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-89815-484-9 |location=Berkeley, CA |pages=91-94}}</ref> and competed for first place for thirty-five weeks.<ref name=":6" /> It was the sixth-best-selling fiction book of 1964,<ref name=":33">{{Cite book |last=Hackett |first=Alice Payne |title=70 Years of Best Sellers, 1895-1965 |date=1967 |publisher=[[R.R. Bowker]] |location=New York |pages=224, 227 |language=}}</ref> and had sold 2 million copies by 1966.{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=155}} However, the novel's chief competitor for end-of-year literary honors, [[Saul Bellow]]'s ''[[Herzog (novel)|Herzog]],'' spent 29 weeks at #1, finished third on the yearly rankings for both 1964 and 1965, and sold considerably more hardcover copies (142,000 to 80,000).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Leader |first=Zachary |date=April 17, 2015 |title=The five essential Saul Bellow novels |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2015/apr/17/the-five-essential-saul-bellow-novels |access-date=April 26, 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name=":33" /><ref name=":32" />

[[Walter Wanger]] [[optioned]] the film rights for [[MGM]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 18, 1964 |title=Spies and Schooldays |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/10/18/archives/new-york-previews-spies-and-schooldays-walter-wanger-to-film-2-new.html?searchResultPosition=5 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiler |first=A. H. |author-link=A. H. Weiler |date=November 1, 1964 |title=New Horizons for Cukor, Niven and Hatfield |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/01/archives/new-york-previews-new-horizons-for-cukor-niven-and-hatfield.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220126/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/01/archives/new-york-previews-new-horizons-for-cukor-niven-and-hatfield.html |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He recruited [[George Cukor]] to direct, [[Samuel A. Taylor]] to write the screenplay, and [[Spencer Tracy]] and [[Katharine Hepburn]] to play the leads. However, Tracy was in poor health and the film was never made.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Curtis |first=James |url= |title=Spencer Tracy |date=2011 |publisher=[[Hutchinson Heinemann|Hutchinson]] |isbn=978-0-09-178524-6 |pages=821–23 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Critical response and awards consideration ===
Critics generally praised the novel. It was a finalist for the [[Pulitzer Prize for Fiction]] and the [[National Book Award for Fiction]], losing to [[Shirley Ann Grau]]'s ''[[The Keepers of the House|The Keeper of the House]]'' and Bellow's ''Herzog'', respectively.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Book Awards 1965 |url=https://www.nationalbook.org/awards-prizes/national-book-awards-1965/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430155636/https://www.nationalbook.org/awards-prizes/national-book-awards-1965/ |archive-date=April 30, 2021 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |website=[[National Book Foundation]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Although Pulitzer jurors Lewis Stiles Gannett and [[Maxwell Geismar]] personally disliked ''Herzog'', they picked ''The Keeper of the House'' over ''The Rector of Justin'' in part because the latter was "precisely ... the kind of novel to which the prize has been awarded in the past".<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last1=Fischer |first1=Heinz-Dietrich |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Yjj7FiO4p44C |title=Chronicle of the Pulitzer Prizes for Fiction: Discussions, Decisions and Documents |last2=Fischer |first2=Erika J. |date=February 14, 2012 |publisher=[[K. G. Saur Verlag]] |isbn=978-3-11-097330-3 |location=Munich |pages=282 |language=en |access-date=September 17, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208091428/https://books.google.com/books?id=Yjj7FiO4p44C |archive-date=December 8, 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Geismar also dismissed Auchincloss' work as insubstantial, explaining that while he typically gave Auchincloss favorable reviews, his books were "polished entertainment and nothing else".<ref name=":8" /> Auchincloss admitted that it was "silly of me to mind" losing the awards, but was wounded nonetheless.<ref name=":6">{{Cite news |last=Plimpton |first=George |author-link=George Plimpton |date=Fall 1994 |title=Louis Auchincloss, The Art of Fiction No. 138 |url=https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/1759/the-art-of-fiction-no-138-louis-auchincloss |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250613170910/https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/1759/the-art-of-fiction-no-138-louis-auchincloss |archive-date=June 13, 2025 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |work=[[The Paris Review]] |language=en |volume= |issue=132 |issn=0031-2037}}</ref>

Despite the award snubs, J. Donald Adams (''[[The New York Times]]''), [[Leon Edel]] (''[[Life (magazine)|Life]]''), and ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine argued that ''The Rector of Justin'' sealed Auchincloss' place in the league of major American novelists.<ref name=":30" /><ref name=":31">{{Cite magazine |last=Edel |first=Leon |author-link=Leon Edel |date=July 17, 1964 |title=Grand Old Man - Not What He Seems To Be |magazine=[[Life (magazine)|Life]] |pages=11, 18 |via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |date=September 4, 1964 |title=Television: Sep. 4, 1964 |url=https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,830547-4,00.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215922/https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,830547-4,00.html |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |language=en-US |issn=0040-781X}}</ref> Auchincloss was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Letters]] the following year,<ref name=":23">{{Cite web |last=Russello |first=Gerald J. |date=2021-05-19 |title=Society vanishes |url=https://newcriterion.com/article/society-vanishes/ |access-date=2025-09-27 |website=[[The New Criterion]] |language=en-US}}</ref> and later served as the Academy's president.<ref name=":0" /> In addition, Paul Pickrel (''[[Harper's Magazine]]'') called the novel "almost certainly the finest work ever written about an American preparatory school",{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=33}} and [[Edmund Fuller]] (''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'') said that ''[[A Separate Peace]]'' was Auchincloss' only competition for the title.{{Sfn|Bryer|1977|p=140}} 

Critics were particularly impressed with Auchincloss' characterization and subtlety of manner. [[Orville Prescott]] (''The New York Times'') called the novel "deeply human," saying it demonstrated an "emotional power and [] psychological fascination ... rarely found in anybody's [work]."<ref name=":28">{{Cite news |last=Prescott |first=Orville |author-link=Orville Prescott |date=July 13, 1964 |title=In Loving Memory of a Noble Failure |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/07/13/archives/books-of-the-times-in-loving-memory-of-a-noble-failure.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215951/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/07/13/archives/books-of-the-times-in-loving-memory-of-a-noble-failure.html |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> [[Stephen Spender]] said that while he thought ''Herzog'' was a more interesting book, "''The Rector of Justin'' is not just another debunking novel about a Victorian prig," because through Auchincloss' detailing of Prescott's internal contradictions, "[f]ew characters in modern fiction have been portrayed so completely in the round."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Spender |first=Stephen |author-link=Stephen Spender |title=The Great Ideas Today 1965 |publisher=[[Encyclopaedia Britannica]] |year=1965 |editor-last=Hutchins |editor-first=Robert M. |editor-link=Robert Maynard Hutchins |location=Chicago |pages=186–87 |chapter=Literature |editor-last2=Adler |editor-first2=Mortimer J. |editor-link2=Mortimer J. Adler}}</ref> Edith Copeland ([[University of Oklahoma]]) was impressed by Auchincloss' "precise, disciplined crystalline prose under perfect control", which had "no need of melodrama".<ref name=":20">{{Cite journal |last=Copeland |first=Edith |date=1965 |title=Fiction in the United States: 1964 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40119565 |journal=Books Abroad |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=151–152 |doi=10.2307/40119565 |issn=0006-7431 |jstor=40119565 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> [[Whitney Balliett]] (''[[The New Yorker]]'') said that Auchincloss had written a "model novel," with "poise and taste and intelligence ... on every page."{{Sfn|Bryer|1977|p=134}} Leon Edel praised the novel for "subtly tak[ing] [its] legends apart before our eyes",<ref name=":31" /> and ''Time'' wrote that "Auchincloss writes in the manner of [[Henry James]], finding great moral dilemmas in small events".<ref>{{Cite magazine |last= |date=July 24, 1964 |title=Books: A Case of Forced Faith |url=https://time.com/archive/6872153/books-a-case-of-forced-faith/ |access-date=April 22, 2025 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |language=en}}</ref>

Reviews were not universally positive, and several commentators argued that Auchincloss should have been more critical of his class. ''[[The New York Review of Books]]'', a brand-new "radical chic" literary magazine published by boarding-school alumnus [[A. Whitney Ellsworth]] ([[St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)|St. Paul's]] '54),{{Sfn|Baltzell|1976|p=509}}{{Efn|During the turbulent 1960s, many of the most radical critics of the status quo were actually WASPs. During the [[1969–1970 Harvard University anti-Vietnam War protests|1969 occupation of Harvard's University Hall]], "approximately 50 percent [of the occupying students who were arrested] attended prep school, with the largest representation from the most exclusive ones"; by way of comparison, 40 percent of the student body were prep school alumni.{{sfn|Baltzell|1976|p=515}}}} panned the novel; its critic [[Robert M. Adams (literary scholar)|Robert M. Adams]] said that Auchincloss' critique of the boarding school system was "fake criticism" and "afraid to ask the questions that hurt".<ref name=":11" /> Leigh Bienen (''[[Transition Magazine|Transition]]'') likewise dismissed the book as "pleasant and not very profound," having achieved commercial popularity by "present[ing] little threat to either reader or author".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bienen |first=Leigh Buchanan |date=1965 |title=New American Fiction |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2934393 |journal=Transition |issue=20 |pages=46–51 |doi=10.2307/2934393 |issn=0041-1191 |jstor=2934393|url-access=subscription }}</ref> More broadly, several critics noted that Auchincloss' books consistently dealt with a small slice of American society.{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=157-58}} 

Artistically, several reviewers, including Edward Weeks (''[[Atlantic Monthly]]''), wrote that the novel's six narrators were too similar;<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weeks |first=Edward |date=July 1964 |title=The Atlantic Bookshelf |url=https://cdn-stage.theatlantic.com/media/archives/1964/07/214-1/132645119.pdf |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The Atlantic]] |pages=132–33 |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220045/https://cdn-stage.theatlantic.com/media/archives/1964/07/214-1/132645119.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Orville Prescott's otherwise laudatory review dryly quipped that "by a happy chance and a familiar literary convention, the six observers are all expert novelists."<ref name=":28" /> Certain aspects of the book were singled out as unrealistic, including the dialogue (Robert Adams)<ref name=":11" /> and Aspinwall's character (''[[Times Literary Supplement]]'').{{Sfn|Bryer|1977|p=149}} Many years later, Auchincloss acknowledged the criticism of his dialogue but protested that "I don't particularly care about having [my characters] talk realistically," because "before the 20th century it really didn't occur to many writers that their language had to be the language of everyday speech. ... I want my characters to get their ideas across, and I want them to be articulate."<ref name="Carrier">{{Cite web |last=Carrier |first=David |author-link=David Carrier |date=October 1, 1997 |title=Interview: Louis Auchincloss |url=https://bombmagazine.org/articles/1997/10/01/louis-auchincloss/ |access-date=September 17, 2025 |website=[[Bomb (magazine)|Bomb]] |language=en}}</ref>
== The end of an era ==
According to one academic, "''The Rector of Justin'' brought its author recognition and popularity, but did little in the long run to secure him a prominent place in postwar American literature".{{sfn|Piket|1989|p=204}} By 1985, ''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]'' noted that Auchincloss "is never mentioned in lists of great American writers" and "has won no important prizes".<ref name=":25">{{Cite magazine |last=Cheever |first=Susan |author-link=Susan Cheever |date=October 1985 |title=The Most Underrated Writer in America |url=https://archive.vanityfair.com/article/1985/10/the-most-underrated-writer-in-america |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220100/https://archive.vanityfair.com/article/1985/10/the-most-underrated-writer-in-america |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |magazine=[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]] |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1995, one critic even said that ''The Rector of Justin'' was the "only [Auchincloss] book to receive substantial critical praise".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=LaHood |first=Marvin J. |date=1995 |title=Review of The Collected Stories of Louis Auchincloss |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40151673 |journal=World Literature Today |volume=69 |issue=4 |pages=789–790 |doi=10.2307/40151673 |issn=0196-3570 |jstor=40151673|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Auchincloss was a four-time finalist for the [[National Book Award for Fiction]], but his last finalist recognition came in 1967.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Louis Auchincloss |url=https://www.nationalbook.org/people/louis-auchincloss/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220037/https://www.nationalbook.org/people/louis-auchincloss/ |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |website=[[National Book Foundation]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== The search for a new fiction ===
''The Rector of Justin'' was published after at least a decade of growing discomfort with [[society novel]]ists. The year the novel was published, [[Howard Mumford Jones]] and Richard M. Ludwig wrote in their ''Guide to American Literature'' that literary fiction had been attracted to a "mood of experimentation" since the mid-1920s. They listed Auchincloss' ''The Great World and Timothy Colt'' (1956) as an example of a novel to which contemporary "[l]iterary histories [were] commonly unkind".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jones |first=Howard Mumford |author-link=Howard Mumford Jones |url= |title=Guide to American Literature and Its Backgrounds since 1890 |last2=Ludwig |first2=Richard M. |date= |publisher=[[Harvard University Press]] |year=1964 |edition=3rd |location=Cambridge, MA |pages=207}}</ref>{{efn|Jones and Ludwig later updated their ''Guide'' to add ''The Rector of Justin'' as a representative example of the modern "conventional" novel.<ref name=":26">{{Cite book |last=Jones |first=Howard Mumford |author-link=Howard Mumford Jones |url= |title=Guide to American Literature and Its Backgrounds since 1890 |last2=Ludwig |first2=Richard M. |date= |publisher=[[Harvard University Press]] |year=1972 |isbn=978-0-674-36753-1 |edition=4th |location=Cambridge, MA |pages=225}}</ref>}} Auchincloss' friend [[Gore Vidal]] added that the literary establishment had been dismissing Auchincloss' style since the early 1950s, and that critics had unfairly criticized him for "never question[ing] [WASP society's] values in any serious way".<ref name=":22" /> 

Auchincloss himself worried that his reputation as a society writer was dragging down both his sales and his critical reputation. In 1953, he urged his publisher [[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt|Houghton Mifflin]] to change its marketing strategy, explaining that "the public that wants 'society' books doesn't want my sort of books. They want something more [[Ouida]] [i.e., melodramatic]. And the others are disgusted by the tag."{{Sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=131-32}} Nor was Auchincloss purely an author of the old school. Even "conventional" writers of the period still employed elements of modernist fiction, such as "a deeper richness of psychology, a distrust of classifying human beings into types, and a greater flexibility of style."<ref name=":26" /> (For example, the Charley Strong section of ''The Rector of Justin'' was Auchincloss' spin on avant-garde prose. Although one scholar called it "easily ... the most uncharacteristic piece of prose" in his career, Auchincloss regarded it with fondness.{{Sfn|Piket|1989|p=193, 320 n.13}}) In any event, starting with ''Pursuit of the Prodigal'' (1959), a finalist for the National Book Award, Auchincloss' critical and commercial reputation began improving, and his books frequently made best-seller lists.{{Sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=148-152}}<ref name=":7" /> ''The House of Five Talents'' (1960) sold 25,000 hardcover copies and was also an NBA finalist.{{Sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=148-152}}

Although ''The Rector of Justin'' was warmly received by audiences and critics, even contemporary reviewers characterized Auchincloss as the last of a dying breed of society author. Virgilia Peterson (''[[The New York Times]]'') wrote that the novel was another example of Auchincloss "imperturbably writing traditional society novels despite the fact that this kind of novel and this society are both supposed to be dead."<ref name=":2" /> Edith Copeland agreed that Auchincloss was one of America's only remaining novelists to concentrate on "well established members of the social order".<ref name=":20" /> A minority of critics hoped that the novel's success could help reverse this trend, and used it to criticize literary and social modernism, including the ''[[Virginia Quarterly Review]]'' (which emphasized the novel's "quiet authority in an age of literary hysteria")<ref>{{Cite journal |date=1964 |title=Notes on Current Books |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/26444881 |journal=[[Virginia Quarterly Review]] |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=cxliv–clxxiv |issn=0042-675X |jstor=26444881}}</ref> and Catholic commentators [[William F. Buckley Jr.]] and [[Edward P. J. Corbett]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Buckley Jr. |first=William F. |author-link=William F. Buckley Jr. |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Let_Us_Talk_of_Many_Things/Zwsu73A3yUsC |title=Let Us Talk of Many Things: The Collected Speeches |date= |publisher=Basic Books |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-7867-2689-9 |edition=2008 paperback |pages=98 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Corbett |first=Edward P. J. |author-link=Edward P. J. Corbett |date=1964-08-08 |title=The Rector of Justin |url=https://wikipedialibrary.idm.oclc.org/login?auth=production&url=https://search.ebscohost.com/login.aspx?direct=true&db=brd&AN=35472730&site=eds-live&scope=site |journal=[[America (magazine)|America Magazine: The Jesuit Review of Faith & Culture]] |volume=111 |issue=6 |pages=140–141}}</ref>

Auchincloss repeatedly argued that his intended audience was much broader than his limited cast of characters. He noted that [[Proust]]'s works also focused on a limited stratum of society<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kachka |first=Boris |date=December 29, 2004 |title=Louis Auchincloss, the Last of the Gentlemen Novelists |url=https://nymag.com/nymetro/arts/books/10790/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240613003911/https://nymag.com/nymetro/arts/books/10790/ |archive-date=June 13, 2024 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |website=[[New York (magazine)|New York Magazine]] |language=en}}</ref> and that non-WASPs like [[Sidney Lumet]] (who he said understood ''The Rector of Justin'' perfectly) could still enjoy his work.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=123}} He admitted that he focused on the New York upper class for convenience, as that background "is a familiar one to me and is hence more available as a model." However, he emphasized that ordinary people could relate to his characters' universal problems, questioning why "critics did not resent [[Anna Karenina]] or [[The Newcomes|Colonel Newcome]]."{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=122}} Gore Vidal added that Auchincloss' society was still relevant in 1960s and 1970s America, and that by downplaying the continuing relevance of WASPs in big business and philanthropy, literary critics revealed their own "remoteness ... from actual power".<ref name=":22" />

| footer            = [[Saul Bellow]]'s ''[[Herzog (novel)|Herzog]]'' beat ''The Rector of Justin'' for the 1965 [[National Book Award for Fiction]]. Bellow's modern writing style and comparatively diverse cast of characters proved more influential than Auchincloss' understated realism.
}} At the end of 1964, Francis Brown (''The New York Times'') drew a distinction between ''The Rector of Justin'' and its awards-season competitor, Bellow's ''Herzog''. He explained that the choice between the two reflected a fork in the road for American literature:<blockquote>"We have writers who adhere in the main to the content, form and style of the novel and short story that are traditional and classic. We have experimentalists, here and abroad, who reject old forms, old styles. There is a conflict of philosophies: belief that life has a purpose, or if it doesn't, at least the living of life can have some joy to it, contends with insistence that there is nothing to life but the living of it, and that even that is absurd. ... [''The Rector of Justin''] is all most absorbing and convincing but it is told in a form that is familiar and in a style that shows no experimental flourish. ... By contrast, [''Herzog''] is as unconventional in its form as in the manner of its telling, and [], to be vulgar about it, packs a fresh and mighty wallop."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Brown |first=Francis |date=1964-12-06 |title=A Sorting Out |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/12/06/archives/a-sorting-out.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220028/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/12/06/archives/a-sorting-out.html |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=2025-04-23 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref></blockquote>Brown was not the only critic to compare the two novels. His ''Times'' colleague J. Donald Adams—a self-avowed traditionalist who believed that the [[novel of manners]] was still "the most interesting form of fiction"—called ''Herzog''<nowiki/>'s victory over ''The Rector of Justin'' a "miscarriage of justice" and Bellow's novel "little more" than "vogue". He added that Auchincloss was "the best living American novelist" and that he had "little confidence" in the generation of modernist authors that included Bellow and [[Norman Mailer]].<ref name=":30">{{Cite book |last=Adams |first=J. Donald |url= |title=Speaking of Books and Life: Selections from the Column that Became an Institution in The New York Times |date= |publisher=[[Rinehart & Company|Holt, Rinehart and Winston]] |year=1966 |location=New York |pages=10-13}}</ref> Mailer, for his own part, opined that "the maudlin middle reaches of ''The Rector of Justin''" represented "the bankruptcy of the novel of manners". He praised the character of Moses Herzog because "it says: I am debased, I am failed, I am near to rotten, and yet something just as good and loving resides in me as the tenderest part of your childhood", and concluded that ''Herzog'' lay "at the center of the modern dilemma".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mailer |first=Norman |author-link=Norman Mailer |date=March 1, 1966 |title=Modes and Mutations: Quick Comments on the Modern American Novel |url=https://www.commentary.org/articles/norman-mailer/modes-and-mutations-quick-comments-on-the-modern-american-novel/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250119172517/https://www.commentary.org/articles/norman-mailer/modes-and-mutations-quick-comments-on-the-modern-american-novel/ |archive-date=January 19, 2025 |access-date=April 26, 2025 |website=[[Commentary (magazine)|Commentary]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

As Mailer alluded, the ''Herzog-Justin'' debate reflected broader disputes about American society. [[Granville Hicks]] admitted that "to many people, myself included ... a bewildered intellectual in search of wholeness of spirit belongs more truly to our times than the aged headmaster of a fashionable preparatory school".{{Sfn|Tuttleton|1998|pp=250-51}} ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' (which at the time "reflected a WASP upper-class point of view"{{Sfn|Baltzell|1976|p=505}}) favored Auchincloss' "Establishment tale" and panned ''Herzog'', while rival ''[[Newsweek]]'' (which catered to urban sophisticates, "underdogs", and fans of the avant-garde) praised ''Herzog'' and mocked ''The Rector of Justin'' for its "tired sentimentality".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Halasz |first=Piri |author-link=Piri Halasz |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/A_Memoir_of_Creativity.html?id=nnp5NZ-gMNcC |title=A Memoir of Creativity: Abstract Painting, Politics & the Media, 1956-2008 |date=2009 |publisher=[[iUniverse]] |isbn=978-1-4401-2322-1 |location=Bloomington, IN |pages=82 |language=en}}</ref> In a further twist of the knife, ''Newsweek'' suggested that pseudo-intellectuals liked reading Auchincloss because he made them feel sophisticated and "educated."{{Sfn|Bryer|1977|p=145}} In his 1966 novel ''Too Far to Walk'', [[John Hersey]] dramatized the conflict by describing ''The Rector of Justin'' as a novel that a college student is assigned to read in a [[political science]] class, in contrast to ''Herzog'', which was assigned in a [[religion and sexuality]] class flippantly dubbed "Totems and Scrotums".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hersey |first=John |author-link=John Hersey |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZredDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22herzog%22+%22rector+of+justin%22&pg=PA139 |title=Too Far to Walk |publisher=[[Vintage Books]] |year=1966 |isbn=978-0-593-08106-8 |edition=2020 |location=New York |pages=139 |language=en}}</ref>

''Herzog'', like many modernist novels of the time, focused on the trials and tribulations of "the American intellectual male".<ref name=":9" /> Auchincloss went in a different direction, and followed up ''The Rector of Justin'' with an essay collection in which he critiqued, as [[Ellen Moers]] (''The New York Times'') summarized, "the dominant (in America) masculine fiction of rootlessness and rejection".<ref name=":29">{{Cite news |last=Moers |first=Ellen |author-link=Ellen Moers |date=1965-07-25 |title=The Creation of Women |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1965/07/25/archives/the-creation-of-women-pioneers-and-caretakers-a-study-of-nine.html |access-date=2025-10-06 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> Drawing from the works of nine American women novelists, he argued that female writers had traditionally provided a "more affirmative note" in American literature,<ref name=":29" /> and that while his subjects agreed that modern society had problems, they still wanted to identify elements worth keeping.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Prescott |first=Orville |author-link=Orville Prescott |date=1965-06-07 |title=Books of the Times: Nine Women Novelists |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1965/06/07/archives/nine-women-novelists.html |access-date=2025-10-06 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> 

=== Modernism triumphant ===
Bellow won the [[1976 Nobel Prize in Literature]]. When the [[Swedish Academy]] presented him with the award, [[Karl Ragnar Gierow]] remarked that he had helped lead the "emancipation from the previous ideal style" in American fiction. Gierow added that Bellow's novels demonstrated "penetrating insight into the outer and inner complications that drive us to act or prevent us from acting and that can be the dilemma of our age."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Saul Bellow: Award ceremony speech |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1976/ceremony-speech/ |access-date=2025-10-07 |website=NobelPrize.org |publisher=[[Swedish Academy]] |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Tracing the development of postwar American literary fiction, Leo Robson (''The New Yorker'') concluded that ''Herzog'' helped "tip[] the balance in favor of the poetic and demotic, the [[Romanticism|Romantic]] and expansive", which in turn prompted critics to downgrade formalist and realist novels like ''The Rector of Justin''.<ref name=":9">{{Cite magazine |last=Robson |first=Leo |date=March 11, 2019 |title=John Williams and the Canon That Might Have Been |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2019/03/18/john-williams-and-the-canon-that-might-have-been |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250110061724/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2019/03/18/john-williams-and-the-canon-that-might-have-been |archive-date=January 10, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |language=en-US |issn=0028-792X}}</ref> Catherine Kord (''[[The Antioch Review]]'') agreed that "with the avant-garde seeking new ways of presenting fiction ... Auchincloss's New York can seem quaint or even marginal."<ref name=":21">{{Cite journal |last=Kord |first=Catherine |date=1995 |title=Review of Tales of Yesteryear |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4613138 |journal=[[The Antioch Review]] |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=236 |doi=10.2307/4613138 |issn=0003-5769 |jstor=4613138 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Time also proved that the women authors Auchincloss courted were also attracted to literary modernism. One writer suggested that by 1989, "the bulk of [American] novelists—male ''and'' female—[were] still closer to [[Barry Hannah]] than they are to Louis Auchincloss."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pinsker |first=Sanford |date=1989 |title=Philip Rahv's "Paleface and Redskin"—Fifty Years Later |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41399927 |journal=[[The Georgia Review]] |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=485 |issn=0016-8386}}</ref> 

Beyond stylistic shifts, Auchincloss was dogged by the perception that novels were not his strong point.{{efn|Auchincloss noted that book publishers of the period were reluctant to publish short story collections, which they deemed bad for business.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Quarles |first=Philip |date=2017-06-15 |title=Louis Auchincloss Talks About His Manhattan |url=https://www.wnyc.org/story/louis-auchincloss-talks-about-his-manhattan/ |access-date=2025-10-11 |website=[[WNYC]] |language=en}}</ref>}} Vidal said that while Auchincloss was a "superb short-story writer", he was merely a "good novelist".<ref name=":22" /> (Norman Mailer, hardly a fan, still envied Auchincloss' short story "The Gemlike Flame."<ref name=":10" />) Merle Rubin (''[[Los Angeles Times]]'') agreed that Auchincloss' short stories generally outstripped his novels, but felt that ''The Rector of Justin'' was an exception and opined that "it hardly seems fair to penalize his productivity by holding his less accomplished books against him".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rubin |first=Merle |date=November 23, 1997 |title=The Atonement and Other Stories |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-nov-23-bk-56832-story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215912/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-nov-23-bk-56832-story.html |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Frank N. Magill (Salem Press) and Mark Oppenheimer (''[[Tablet (magazine)|Tablet]]'') wrote that Auchincloss' post-''Justin'' works tended to recycle the ''Justin'' formula, which (in Magill's words) "threaten[ed] to undermine, even in retrospect, the reputation justly earned by his best work."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Magill |first=Frank N. |title=Critical Survey of Long Fiction: Authors A-Cald |publisher=Salem Press |year=1983 |isbn=978-0-89356-360-8 |location=Englewood Cliffs, NJ |pages=112–13}}</ref><ref name=":27">{{Cite web |last=Oppenheimer |first=Mark |date=February 20, 2008 |title=Tales from School |url=https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/arts-letters/articles/tales-from-school |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220221/https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/arts-letters/articles/tales-from-school |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |website=[[Tablet (magazine)|Tablet]] |language=en}}</ref> Auchincloss' prolific output also attracted criticism:<ref name=":18" />{{Sfn|Dahl|1986|p=245}} he published roughly one book a year, and admitted that he could have taken more time revising his works.<ref name="Cornwell" />  

Other critics blamed politics for Auchincloss' comparative slide into obscurity. Gerald Russello (''[[The New Criterion]]'') opined that "because Auchincloss did not explicitly disdain the WASPs, he didn't ascend to that league of writers dutifully 'problematizing' formerly standard American tropes."<ref name=":23" /> [[Bruce Bawer]] (''The New York Times'') argued that modern critics ignored Auchincloss not just because his viewpoints were unpopular, but because "the questions [Auchincloss asks] themselves are politically incorrect; they concern social facts that we're supposed to pretend nowadays not to notice."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bawer |first=Bruce |author-link=Bruce Bawer |date=1994-12-04 |title=Requiem for the Upper Crust |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/12/04/books/requiem-for-the-upper-crust.html |access-date=2025-09-27 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en}}</ref>  

Auchincloss predicted his own critical decline, but was unable to stop it. During the 1965 awards season, he told Gore Vidal that "the year of ''The Rector of Justin'' had given way to the glorious era of ''Herzog'' and we are now dim figures of a gentile American past". He concluded that "we had our day, and though we lacked Moral Seriousness, in our Waspish way, we had style."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bloom |first=James D. |date=1998 |title=For the Yankee Dead: Mukherjee, Roth, and the Diasporan Seizure of New England |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41201358 |journal=Studies in American Jewish Literature |volume=17 |pages=41 |issn=0271-9274 |jstor=41201358}}</ref>

== Modern appraisals ==
''The Rector of Justin'' is generally considered Auchincloss' best work.{{efn|For example, see the following sources.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":21" />{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=9, 13}}<ref>{{Cite web |last=Begley |first=Louis |author-link=Louis Begley |title=Tribute to Louis Auchincloss |url=https://www.artsandletters.org/tributes/louis-auchincloss |access-date=April 23, 2025 |website=American Academy of Arts and Letters |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":18" />}} In 2008, [[Larissa MacFarquhar]] (''[[The New Yorker]]'') wrote that ''The Rector of Justin'' was Auchincloss' masterpiece "because it is one of the few times he permits his elegiac moralism to dominate a book. He loves his mad Puritans, and believes they are no more."<ref name=":13" /> In her 1993 biography of Auchincloss, Carol Gelderman wrote that it was one of Auchincloss' three best works, along with ''The House of Five Talents'' and ''Portrait in Brownstone''.{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=221}}

Auchincloss enjoyed a brief critical revival in the 1980s.{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=10}} In 1977, Jackson Bryer assembled an extensive bibliography of Auchincloss' career, including a list of book reviews from around the world. This was followed by two book-length academic studies of Auchincloss' career by [[Christopher Dahl (administrator)|Christopher Dahl]] and David Parsell and a dissertation by {{Interlanguage link|彭家傑|lt=Vincent Piket|zh}}. Parsell proclaimed that ''The Rector of Justin'' was "unquestionably" the best American boarding school novel.{{sfn|Parsell|1988|p=52}} The new critics challenged Auchincloss' reputation for inaccessibility to ordinary Americans, with Bryer pointing out that "local book editors ... have been his most consistent and enthusiastic supporters."{{sfn|Bryer|1977|p=xi}}<ref name=":25" /> Dahl and [[Susan Cheever]] (''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]'') also recognized Auchincloss' sympathy for and depiction of the lives of women;{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=21-22}}<ref name=":25" /> Cheever explained that Auchincloss was "one of a handful of male writers whose sympathy for women is so extraordinary that his female characters are as complete and convincing as his men."<ref name=":25" /> At the end of the decade, [[Whit Stillman]]'s 1990 film ''[[Metropolitan (1990 film)|Metropolitan]]'' used the novel as a metonym for a new generation of upper-crust Americans’ "self-questioning and unease at the perspective of social decline and a descent into irrelevance."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zagha |first=Muriel |date=June 10, 2025 |title=Whit Stillman's comedies of manners |url=https://engelsbergideas.com/notebook/whit-stillmans-comedies-of-manners/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250904233619/https://engelsbergideas.com/notebook/whit-stillmans-comedies-of-manners/ |archive-date=September 4, 2025 |access-date=September 17, 2025 |website=Engelsberg ideas |language=}}</ref> However, not all the attention was positive. [[Michiko Kakutani]] (''The New York Times'') concluded in 1984 that "while [Auchincloss] is adept enough at portraying the effects of a rarified milieu on character, his narrative lacks a necessary density and texture."<ref name="Kakutani" /> Dahl coupled his praise of ''Justin'' with critiques of Auchincloss' later career, which Auchincloss still fumed about a decade later.<ref name="Carrier" />

In the 21st century, [[Michael Tolkin]] (''[[Los Angeles Review of Books]]'') and Mark Oppenheimer (''[[Tablet (magazine)|Tablet]]'') expressed a renewed interest in Auchincloss' writing style. Tolkin opined that his deliberately understated delivery obscured the full depth of his characters, like how a lawyer would "seal[] ... the most exciting material behind attorney-client privilege".<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Tolkin |first=Michael |author-link=Michael Tolkin |date=May 9, 2011 |title=One Inch Above the Ground |url=https://lareviewofbooks.org/article/one-inch-above-the-ground/ |access-date=April 22, 2025 |website=[[Los Angeles Review of Books]]}}</ref> Oppenheimer embraced how Auchincloss' prose could be from "1920, or 1940—some imagined time when sentences had the leisure to amble around, tasting and then regurgitating highbrow references and allusions, not rushing to any forced conclusion."<ref name=":27" /> Although he did not consider Auchincloss a great writer in general,<ref name=":27" /> he predicted that ''The Rector of Justin'' would "someday be recognized as a classic."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Oppenheimer |first=Mark |date=February 1, 2005 |title=An Era of Awkward Obsession |url=https://www.thebeliever.net/an-era-of-awkward-obsession/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215958/https://www.thebeliever.net/an-era-of-awkward-obsession/ |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |website=[[The Believer (magazine)|The Believer]] |language=en-US}}</ref>{{Quote box
| quote = Auchincloss just seems to have such painful nostalgia for this world .... Intellectually, [he] knows that his heroes, these characters he loves, are morally bad, or at least limited. But he finds them beautiful anyway, and he mourns their passing.

Many of us do, I think. Now that Jews have been admitted to the club, we discover that it's a rip-off, with bad food and overpriced drinks. There's a poignant sense that maybe, in another time, it really was glamorous, that once we were being excluded from something worth having. The morality was bad, but the aesthetic was grand.
| author = Mark Oppenheimer<ref name=":27" />
| align = right
| width = 300px
}}

Auchincloss' death in 2010 prompted a new round of revisionist reflections, which acknowledged his cutting social commentary and, in some cases, used nostalgia for Auchincloss' WASPs to criticize the new American elite. Eric Homberger (''[[The Guardian]]'') remembered him for "interrogat[ing] the values, class consciousness and self-representations of the most powerful people in the world's most powerful nation."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Homberger |first=Eric |date=2010-01-28 |title=Louis Auchincloss obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2010/jan/28/louis-auchincloss-obituary |access-date=2025-10-11 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Boris Kachka (''[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]]'') similarly hailed him as the "conscience of an elite", writing
